questions.question: With initial condition x(1)=0.5, the solution of the differential equation [latex]t\frac{dx}{dt}+x=t[/latex], is
questions.explanation: The given differential equation is [latex]\frac{tdx}{dt}+x=t[/latex] with initial condition [latex]x(t)=\frac{1}{2}[/latex] which is same as  [latex]\frac{dx}{dt}+\frac{x}{t}=1[/latex] Which is a linear differential equation [latex]\frac{dx}{dt}+P{x}=Q[/latex] Where,  [latex]P=\frac{1}{t}[/latex] and Q=1 Integrating factor [latex]=e^{\int P\;dt}=e^{\int \frac{1}{t}dt}=e^{\log _{e}t}=t[/latex] Solution  is [latex]\begin{aligned} x\cdot (IF) &=\int Q\cdot (IF)dt +C\\ x\cdot t&= \int 1\cdot t\cdot dt+C\\ xt&= \frac{t^2}{2}+C\\ x&= \frac{t}{2}+\frac{C}{t}\\ \text{Put } x(1)&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \; \frac{1}{2}+\frac{C}{1}&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \; C&=0 \\ \text{So, }x&=\frac{t}{2}\text{ is the solution.} \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
The given differential equation is [latex]\frac{tdx}{dt}+x=t[/latex] with initial condition [latex]x(t)=\frac{1}{2}[/latex] which is same as [latex]\frac{dx}{dt}+\frac{x}{t}=1[/latex]
Which is a linear differential equation
[latex]\frac{dx}{dt}+P{x}=Q[/latex]
Where, [latex]P=\frac{1}{t}[/latex] and Q=1
Integrating factor [latex]=e^{\int P\;dt}=e^{\int \frac{1}{t}dt}=e^{\log _{e}t}=t[/latex]
Solution is

questions.question: Given that [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} -5 &-3 \\ 2&0 \end{bmatrix} \; and \; I=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex], the value of [latex]A^{3}[/latex] is
questions.explanation: [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} -5 & -3\\ 2& 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] and [latex]I=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] Characteristic equation of A is [latex]\begin{bmatrix} -5-\lambda & -3\\ 2& 0-\lambda \end{bmatrix}=0[/latex] [latex] (-5-\lambda )(-\lambda )+6=0 [/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \;\; \lambda ^2+5\lambda +6=0 [/latex] [latex]\text{So,  } A^2+5A+6I=0 [/latex] (by Cayley Hamilton theorem) [latex]\Rightarrow \;\; A^2=-5A-6I [/latex] Multiplying by A on both sides, we have, [latex]A^3=-5A^2-6A[/latex] [latex] \Rightarrow \;\; A^3=-5(-5A-6I)-6A=19A+30I[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
[latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} -5 & -3\\ 2& 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] and [latex]I=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Characteristic equation of A is
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} -5-\lambda & -3\\ 2& 0-\lambda \end{bmatrix}=0[/latex]
[latex] (-5-\lambda )(-\lambda )+6=0 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\; \lambda ^2+5\lambda +6=0 [/latex]
[latex]\text{So, } A^2+5A+6I=0 [/latex]
(by Cayley Hamilton theorem)
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\; A^2=-5A-6I [/latex]
Multiplying by A on both sides, we have,
[latex]A^3=-5A^2-6A[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \;\; A^3=-5(-5A-6I)-6A=19A+30I[/latex]
